title: Volume of Cones
short: A cone holds one third of the matching cylinder.
trouble: Students forget the 1/3, or use the slant height.

blocks.html: A cone has a circle for a base, like a cylinder, but it narrows to a point. How much less does it hold?

Fill a cone with water and pour it into a cylinder with the same base and the same height. It takes exactly three cones to fill the cylinder. So a cone holds one third of its matching cylinder. (The same is true for a pyramid and its prism; a careful proof comes in calculus.)

blocks.name: g8-solid
blocks.cap: Pour cones of water into the cylinder with the same base and height.

blocks.html: $$V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2} h$$ where $h$ is the height measured straight up from the center of the base, not the slant height along the side.

blocks.title: Radius and height
blocks.q: A cone has radius 3 and height 4. Find its volume.

blocks.title: Given the slant height
blocks.q: A cone has radius 6 cm and slant height 10 cm. Find its volume.
steps: Height, radius and slant height form a right triangle: $h^{2} + 6^{2} = 10^{2}$, so $h = 8$.

blocks.name: g8-solid
blocks.cap: The slant height (gold) runs along the side. The height (dashed) goes straight up the middle.

blocks.title: Compare with a cylinder
blocks.q: A cylinder holds $90\pi$ cubic inches. How much does a cone with the same base and height hold?
steps: A cone is one third of the matching cylinder: $90\pi \div 3$.

blocks.html: Forgetting the $\frac{1}{3}$, which gives the volume of the whole cylinder, or using the slant height as $h$. The height must be perpendicular to the base; if you are given the slant height, use the Pythagorean theorem to find $h$ first.
